data.title: Same AI price, very different costs: what to automate in South-east Asia
data.description:
A CUSTOMER opens a chat to dispute a charge. Resolving it takes a staff member about 20 minutes.

In Singapore, that costs the company about US$7.90. In Indonesia, it costs about US$0.60.

Yet, a leading customer service software firm charges the same price in both markets for an artificial intelligence agent to handle that chat.

Board members across South-east Asia are now asking their executive teams which workflows to hand to AI agents.

Our answer is that the business case depends on where the work is done. We compare the cost of the staff who do the work today with the cost of the AI that would do it instead.

The cost of a workflow

We cover six markets: Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines and Indonesia. Our staff costs are based on official wage data for clerical or similar roles, and a 50 per cent addition for employer contributions, supervision and tools.

One customer service software firm charges from US$0.99 each time its AI agent resolves a chat. But AI agents may not be fully autonomous in customer service, so our calculations factor in human staff costs.

The same software firm reports that its AI agent resolves three chats in four on average. Results vary widely by business, so we assume a more cautious scenario, where the AI resolves six chats in 10. Staff still handle the other four.

The human part of the job then moves from routine handling to reviewing and deciding. The staff checks one in 10 chats, taking three minutes each time.

For a business handling 20,000 chats a month, we assume half a full-time employee is required just to manage and maintain the agent.

By our calculations, at US$0.99 per outcome and even after a business pays for the staff it still needs, an AI agent cuts the cost of a chat in Singapore by about half.

In Malaysia, it cuts the cost by about a quarter, and in Thailand by about a tenth. In Vietnam, it saves nothing. In the Philippines and Indonesia, it adds to the cost.

These figures are illustrative estimates based on a single workflow and average wages, which mask wide variances between firms. In reality too, large clients often negotiate published prices down.

Our calculation also excludes the cost of building an agent, connecting it to existing systems and keeping it up to date as models change.

Businesses must therefore run the math using their own data.

The success rate matters too. If the agent resolves only half of all chats, the savings in Singapore fall to about 40 per cent.

If the agent resolves three in four, the savings rise to about 60 per cent. Singapore still saves the most and Indonesia still loses the most.

The reference firm charges for each chat its agent resolves. In higher-wage markets where staff cost more than about US$1 a chat, an agent with a higher resolution rate saves more money.

But where staff costs less, as in the Philippines and Indonesia, every extra chat the agent resolves actually adds to the cost.

The “build vs buy” variable

Some firms build their own agents rather than buy one from a vendor. For them, the choice of AI model matters a great deal.

For this scenario, we estimated costs for six leading models, based on their published prices. (Models we studied were Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 3.8 Flash, GLM-5.2, DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen 3.5.)

With the cheapest model, the self-built AI agent costs less than staff in every market. With the most expensive, it costs more everywhere except Singapore.

Engineering also makes a difference. When building an agent, design can directly affect the bottom line.

Take a mid-priced model: an agent that wastefully rereads twice as much company material at every step would lose its savings in Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines and Indonesia.

An agent engineered to cache material, instead of rereading it, would pay off in all six markets.

Does running AI locally shift the case?

Today, most AI models run in a few giant data centres, mostly outside South-east Asia, and are sold at one global price.

As more countries insist on data sovereignty, keeping data and AI processing at home, more AI is likely to run locally. It would then carry local costs, including power and the cost of meeting each country’s rules and regulations.

Power is the easiest of these costs to measure. Electricity for a data centre costs about three times as much in Singapore as in Indonesia. Still, that makes the same AI only about 10 per cent more expensive.

By contrast, staff costs nearly 13 times as much. So even if AI runs locally, wages are likely to decide where AI agents make commercial sense. The cost of compliance is the open question.

Moving prices and looking beyond costs

Leading AI companies currently spend far more than they earn.

OpenAI expects to burn through about US$280 billion between 2026 and 2030, according to company projections reported by the Financial Times.

Prices may therefore rise. On our estimates, if a mid-priced model trebled its token prices, the savings from AI would disappear everywhere in South-east Asia except Singapore.

Exchange rates add a second risk. AI prices are set in US dollars. A weaker ringgit, baht, dong or rupiah makes the AI agent more expensive in local terms, while local salaries stay roughly the same.

Still, costs may not be the only consideration. AI agents work around the clock; they can absorb sudden peaks in demand, help launch new services faster and create new ways to serve customers.

Where an AI agent saves little in operating costs, these benefits could still justify deploying one.

What leaders should do

Start with the process. Map each workflow and remove unnecessary steps. Every step an AI agent performs adds cost.

Then ask three simple questions of each workflow: One, what does it cost us today? Two, what will it cost with an AI agent, including the staff it still needs? Three, how far could AI prices rise, or the local currency fall, before the business case fails?

Answer these questions separately for each market. Where the savings are small or negative, name the other benefits you expect in advance and measure them.

Crucially, businesses should keep the decision reversible for as long as possible.

Once teams are reshaped around AI agents, the know-how to do the work without them may be lost, and rebuilding that is slow and costly.

A phased roll-out is sensible. Each phase shows what the agent can handle before more of the workflow depends on it.

Avoid tying the workflow to a single provider or model. If that provider changes its terms, retires a model or fails, the business should be able to switch without starting over.

AI may cost the same in every market, but the case for it is won or lost, workflow by workflow and market by market.

Daniel Liebau is an adjunct associate professor with the Asian Institute of Digital Finance at the National University of Singapore, and the founding managing director of Lightbulb Capital, an innovation advisory firm. Damien Kopp is the founder and managing director of RebootUp, an AI advisory firm, and associate faculty, executive development, at Singapore Management University.

Workings are available from the authors on request.

data.title: Singapore is winning the HQ race. Is it winning the leadership race?
data.description:
SINGAPORE now hosts about 1,030 foreign headquarters, up from roughly 770 in 2019. Over the same period, the resident professionals, managers and executives (PMEs) working in them grew by less than 8 per cent, from 12,700 to 13,700, as The Straits Times reported recently.

The explanation on offer is reassuring. A regional headquarters today, one adviser told the paper, is often “a leaner set-up focused on senior decision-making”, while operational roles move to cheaper markets.

That may well be true. The problem is that nobody measures it. Singapore counts its headquarters well. It does not yet count what they decide.

What the numbers miss

The PME figures also leave out foreign professionals, so headcount was never the right test of a headquarters. What matters is whether decision-making authority grew alongside the count. On that, the published figures are silent.

The Economic Strategy Review, published in June 2026, wants Singapore’s own companies to keep “headquarters, strategy and decision-making” functions here as they expand abroad, and foreign investors to make Singapore “a critical node” in their operations.

A headquarters, in the sense that counts for an economy, is where decisions are made. For a startup that re-domiciles here, that means where its chief executive and senior team sit.

Flipkart, founded in Bengaluru and serving customers across India, was incorporated in Singapore for 15 years before completing its move back to India in March 2026, ahead of a planned listing.

Throughout that time, Flipkart’s operations stayed in India alongside its executive leadership, while the Singapore headquarters focused on raising capital.

Grab offers a counter-example. Founded in Malaysia, the startup uses its Singapore headquarters as a control centre to manage localised teams across eight South-east Asian markets.

For a multinational’s regional headquarters, the test is narrower. In matrix organisations, few regional heads own every budget.

Even as global head offices hold ultimate control over bigger budgets, genuine regional headquarters can exert strategic influence and anchor a high-value ecosystem of professional services. For this, local leaders require sufficient autonomy.

Can the leaders here approve investment in the region, hire their own team and stop a project without needing a flight to the head office?

The Swiss mirror

Switzerland, where I am based, shows how control can move while the address stays.

Switzerland’s two federal technology universities, ETH in Zurich and EPFL in Lausanne, each produced a record number of new companies in 2025. But Swiss investors supplied at most about 13 per cent of later-stage capital for local startups that year, the Swiss Scale-Up Report 2026 found.

Growth money comes mostly from abroad.

Nexthink, an EPFL spin-off, is a Swiss success story. It still names Lausanne as one of its two headquarters. Its founder and chief executive, however, lives in the Boston area, and in October 2025, the company agreed to sell a majority stake to the American investor Vista Equity Partners.

On paper, Nexthink remains a Swiss-headquartered company. Where its biggest decisions are now taken is a different question.

That is also the risk Singapore faces: A company can maintain its official address in the country long after its true centre of decision-making has moved abroad.

When authority stays at home

In one executive search I handled, a company hired a Singapore-based leader for their understanding of the Asean market.

Yet headquarters, thousands of kilometres away, controlled the expansion budgets, assuming that what worked at home would work in the region.

The hire left for a direct competitor after 14 months, telling me that the lack of decision-making authority was the reason. The company had recruited local judgment but left it little room to act.

Retaining control overseas cost the company the local expertise it had recruited for its regional hub.

Singapore may get the leadership role, but does the authority move with it?

It can go the other way. In October 2026, Nike said the leadership team for a combined Asia-Pacific and Greater China region would be based in Singapore from fiscal year 2028, with some roles moving from its US headquarters.

Whether moves such as that bring real decision rights with them is exactly what Singapore should be tracking.

Closing the gap

Three changes would help.

First, measure authority as well as addresses. Singapore already counts its foreign headquarters and the resident PMEs in them. It could also survey whether those headquarters hold budget and hiring authority for the region, and publish the results in aggregate.

For startups that re-domicile, it could track where the chief executive and senior team are based.

Second, tie incentives to actual decision-making rights.

Today’s international headquarters award counts skilled jobs and local spending. Managing the group from Singapore is one qualifying activity among several, but it is not required.

As Singapore reviews its incentives for the era of the global minimum tax, awards could give weight to whether a regional chief executive or finance chief is a tax resident here and holds the regional budget.

Third, companies should move authority along with the address.

A startup that re-domiciles for capital or neutrality, while keeping every senior role elsewhere, has bought an address. A multinational that hires a regional leader here but signs off every budget at home has bought a title.

Businesses that put real decisions here, give regional leaders real budgets, and hire the next layer locally get what the address was meant to bring: proximity to regional customers, a deeper pool of talent and credibility with the investors who now concentrate their money here.

Singapore has already won the argument about where companies in this region want to be registered. The harder contest is about where they are run from.

To stay the region’s launchpad in 2027 and beyond, Singapore should count not only its headquarters, but also what they are allowed to decide.

The writer is the founder of Gunia Consulting, an advisory and executive search firm for organisation and leadership, with mandates in Europe and Asia, including Singapore. He is based in Zurich.

Views expressed here are his own. He used AI tools for research and editing before submitting the draft.

data.title: Trump pushes for reluctant Xi to curb Chinaâs nuclear arsenal
data.description:
PRESIDENT Donald Trump said he would like China to stop building up its nuclear arsenal, a request that Xi Jinping is almost certain to rebuff if it’s brought up during an unprecedented trilateral meeting including the two leaders and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.

Trump has long pushed for China to join nuclear talks alongside the US and Russia in hopes of controlling the arms race as Beijing moves to rapidly increase its own stockpile. Yet China has dismissed those entreaties, given that its arsenal is much smaller than those of Russia and the US.

“China’s third, a distant third,” Trump said in an interview with Fox News. “But they’re going, you know, they’re going hot and heavy on building nuclear weapons. I’d love them not to do it.”

Trump’s comments indicate that he’s looking to advance the issue during the three-way meeting on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen even though there is little likelihood of a diplomatic breakthrough.

Asked if he would propose having inspections in all three countries, Trump responded: “Yeah, I think it’s fine” and touted his “great relationships” with the other leaders.

He acknowledged the difficulty in convincing China to curb the growth of its nuclear arsenal.

“When they look at me and they say, ‘OK, we’ll do it,’ but will you reduce your nuclear weapons by 2,000 weapons?,” Trump said. “You don’t need 4,000, but it’s a hard thing to do for me. It’s a hard thing. And it’s probably hard for them to do also.” BLOOMBERG

data.title: How should success of Singaporeâs IPO market be defined?
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Something is decidedly odd about celebrating the revival of Singapore’s initial public offering market when the majority of new listings in 2026 are trading below their offer prices, despite the Straits Times Index hitting numerous record highs this year.

As at early November, seven of the 12 new listings on the Singapore Exchange (SGX) were underwater.

Yet, the industry continues to trumpet the number of listings, the amount of capital raised and the supposed resurgence of interest in Singapore stocks.

So, how exactly should IPO success be measured?

Is it a success when shares are fully or oversubscribed, in which case companies raise their targeted capital and intermediaries collect their fees?

Is it when investment bankers are happy and the exchange can chalk up another listing?

Or should success be evaluated from the viewpoint of investors?

An uncomfortable question follows: Is the local IPO market structured primarily for major shareholders and early investors to cash out and intermediaries to earn their fees – at the expense of the investing public?

Consider the incentives involved.

Issuers and vendors naturally want the highest possible prices for their shares.

Investment bankers and issue managers are incentivised to complete transactions as quickly as possible, since fees are generally linked to the size and successful execution of offerings.

Investors, meanwhile, want precisely the opposite – to buy shares at reasonable valuations (read: low prices) that offer scope for meaningful capital appreciation.

Of course, there is nothing inherently wrong or improper about these competing objectives, because that is how capital markets operate.

But when the overwhelming majority of new listings flop as they have this year – and many, very quickly after their debut – surely, it is reasonable to question whether the balance has tilted too far towards the sellers.

Perhaps, those responsible for bringing companies to market should have skin in the game after the IPO bell rings.

Stated differently: Is there any way to ensure part of an issue manager’s remuneration is dependent on post-listing performance over, say, six to 12 months?

Mechanics aside, the underlying principle is accountability.

A publicly accessible scorecard tracking the performance of IPOs, sorted by issue managers, over different periods – six months, one year, three years and so on – would support this.

Such information would allow investors to distinguish between intermediaries with a consistent record of bringing reasonably priced companies to market, and those whose offerings regularly disappoint.

Importantly, these questions come at a time when the IPO process is being streamlined, with SGX RegCo assuming prospectus review functions from 2027.

Efforts to reduce unnecessary regulatory friction are commendable, but making it easier and faster for companies to list should not become an end in itself.

The success of the ongoing Equity Market Development Programme should not be measured by the number of IPOs attracted to SGX, because investor confidence cannot be manufactured through promotional campaigns, fancy listing ceremonies and impressive subscription rates.

It should be earned through credible, quality companies, fair pricing and satisfactory long-term returns.

After all, what is the point of reviving Singapore’s IPO market if the principal beneficiaries are everyone except the investors who finance it?

data.title: Low-profile VCs set for US$100 billion windfall from Anthropic IPO
data.description:
ANTHROPIC’S initial public offering on Thursday (Nov 19) will reorder Silicon Valley’s power rankings, with a small group of venture capitalists who bet early and aggressively on the artificial intelligence lab set for a combined windfall of well over US$100 billion.

Anthropic is expected to be valued at US$1.4 trillion or more when it lists. That would be about 2,300 times its value when Anjney Midha — an angel investor and founder of AMP — first backed the company in 2021.

His company is among a handful of lesser-known groups primed for massive returns at multiples that would surpass those of larger, blue-chip rivals. Others include Spark Capital, which would own about US$11 billion of stock at a US$1.4 trillion valuation, and Factorial Funds, which would own just over US$10 billion, according to calculations by Financial Times.

Spark’s Yasmin Razavi and Factorial’s Sol Bier invested in Anthropic’s Series C funding round, which closed in 2023, when the company was valued at about US$4 billion. Razavi sits on Anthropic’s board.

Anthropic is expected to price its shares after the US stock market closes on Wednesday, with trading set to start on Thursday.

Meanwhile, the manager of pop superstar Madonna, Guy Oseary, stands to net more than US$7 billion from an early investment of just over US$400 million.

“The deck chairs are shifting around in the VC landscape,” said a partner at one mid-sized venture capital (VC) firm which stands to make billions of dollars. “The leaders in the AI wave are not the same as they were in the previous waves. Different firms are moving up the leader board, and we’re glad to be among them.”

Amazon and Google, which have provided investment and computing resources to Anthropic, will collectively own close to 30 per cent of the company after the IPO.

The largest financial investor in the company, Iconiq Capital, holds a fraction of that. Nevertheless, its stake would be worth about US$28 billion at a US$1.4 trillion valuation.

It is followed by Lightspeed Ventures — which has invested roughly US$3.2 billion for a stake worth just over US$25 billion at the same valuation — and Menlo Ventures, which stands to return US$21 billion from an initial US$1 billion investment.

Coatue and Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund GIC invested later, but went big. The pair led a funding round earlier this year which valued Anthropic at US$380 billion, and have each put close to US$5 billion into the company.

Those stakes would be worth more than US$10 billion at an IPO price of US$1.4 trillion.

Sound Ventures, which was founded by Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher, and Bessemer Venture Partners are each poised for returns of about US$7 billion. For Bessemer, that would mark an eight-times increase on its initial investment, while Sound stands to make roughly 17 times its outlay.

Even those massive multiples are dwarfed, though, by the roughly 70-times return jailed crypto-exchange founder Sam Bankman-Fried would have made, if his company had not been forced to sell its US$500 million stake in bankruptcy proceedings in 2024. That stake would be worth about US$35 billion at an IPO price of US$1.4 trillion.

The clamour to own a stake in the AI company has increased in the past year, as the group’s revenues have leapfrogged rival OpenAI.

A partner at one of Anthropic’s large investors said they “wrote (chief financial officer Krishna Rao) a love letter” as they jostled for access to a funding round earlier this year.

The take-off prompted OpenAI’s investors, including Brad Gerstner’s Altimeter, Sequoia Capitaland Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund, to pour money into Anthropic, an unusual move in Silicon Valley, where VCs tend to back a single company in each field and founders prize fealty.

Other big-name venture firms, including Thrive Capital and Andreessen Horowitz, skipped Anthropic entirely.

“Call us old school... but we are serial monogamists,” said Josh Kushner, founder of Thrive, which is one of OpenAI’s largest and most vocal backers, in a since-deleted post on X.

Andreessen’s partners and Anthropic’s executives, meanwhile, have clashed over how best to regulate AI.

A successful IPO would also make thousands of Anthropic employees multimillionaires.

However, the company’s executives have framed fundraising as a necessary evil in the pursuit of their mission to responsibly “develop advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity”.

While its investors celebrate once-in-a-lifetime returns, Anthropic’s leadership is plotting a low-key IPO.

The company has no plans for a party to celebrate the listing and intends to keep fanfare around what is set to be the biggest listing fundraiser of all time to a minimum, said people with knowledge of the matter. FINANCIAL TIMES

data.title: Stocks to watch: Yangzijiang Shipbuilding, Seatrium, Frencken
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 19):

Yangzijiang Shipbuilding : The shipbuilder’s subsidiary has entered into an investment agreement with China’s Taicang Port Economic and Technological Development Zone. The agreement is in relation to a project to develop a clean energy vessel intelligent manufacturing base in Taicang city, located in Jaingsu province. The group expects capital expenditure for the project to be about 3.38 billion yuan (US$507 million). Shares of Yangzijiang Shipbuilding ended 1.6 per cent or S$0.07 higher at S$4.39 on Wednesday, before the announcement.

Seatrium : The offshore, marine and energy specialist reported that its net order book stood at S$12.2 billion as at end-September, comprising 35 projects with deliveries extending through 2033. It had secured S$1.7 billion in new orders so far this year. Seatrium expects its underlying net profit for FY2026 to be materially higher than in FY2025. The counter ended 0.6 per cent or S$0.01 lower at S$1.71, before the news.

Frencken : The technology manufacturer announced on Wednesday (Nov 18) a 31.3 per cent year-on-year increase in earnings to S$13 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30. Revenue grew 12.8 per cent to S$238.5 million, from S$211.5 million a year earlier. The increase was mainly driven by Frencken’s mechatronics division’s revenue, which rose 13.4 per cent to S$214.3 million. The counter ended S$0.01, or 0.6 per cent, up at S$1.71 before the news.

data.title: MAS to develop âKnow Your Agentâ protocol for customer agents and financial institutionsÂ
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] As artificial intelligence agents move into activities with financial consequences, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) will facilitate the development of a Know Your Agent (KYA) protocol for information exchange between customer agents and financial institutions.

“We are at an early stage of agentic use, but adoption has the potential to scale rapidly, and we should start thinking about the potential impact on financial institutions, business models, on markets, and the broad economy,” said MAS managing director Chia Der Jiun on Thursday (Nov 19).

While some financial institutions are building agent interfaces into their offerings, many have yet to establish terms or channels for agents to access financial services, he noted at the Singapore Fintech Festival 2026.

“Some users are giving agents their login credentials to financial accounts. I would not advise giving personal agents such access, as there is insufficient assurance of safety,” he added. 

Against this backdrop, the KYA protocol will cover: who the agent is, whom it represents, what authority it has been given, what mandate it operates under, and what assurance exists about its provenance and reliability. 

“This gives financial institutions the information needed to determine the terms and scope permitted to an agent,” said Chia.

The development of this protocol follows the Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime framework published by MAS earlier this year which contains lessons relevant to how customer agents should transact safely with financial institutions.

data.title: Malaysia to review leaked Deutsche Bank 1MDB files, task force official says
data.description:
[KUALA LUMPUR] Malaysia is studying leaked files that allegedly show that Deutsche Bank ignored internal red flags to help move millions of dollars linked to fugitive financier Low Taek Jho, a senior official said on Wednesday (Nov 18).

News portal Malaysiakini reported that Deutsche Bank’s correspondent banking service was used to facilitate at least 24 transactions worth 172.98 million euros that were linked to Low, a key player in the multibillion-dollar 1Malaysia Development Berhad scandal.

The portal cited leaked internal files from the “Inside Deutsche Bank” investigation, which covers more than 15 million files dating from the early 2010s.

The report also stated that the bank continued to process millions of euros in transfers linked to Low in 2015, despite filing its own suspicious activity reports.

Reuters was unable to independently verify the documents.

A spokesperson for Deutsche Bank said in an email response that the bank has cooperated fully with regulatory and law enforcement authorities in relation to inquiries concerning 1MDB, and has not been subject to any regulatory penalty or sanction arising from 1MDB.

“As stated in asset forfeiture complaints filed by the US Department of Justice, 1MDB made material misrepresentations and omissions to Deutsche Bank officials in connection with 1MDB’s transactions with the bank,” the spokesperson said.

The chairman of the task force in charge of recovering 1MDB assets, Johari Abdul Ghani, told Reuters that the relevant parties, including the task force itself and 1MDB’s legal team, were now studying the information.

However, he said it was still “premature” to comment on Malaysia’s position while the court case against Deutsche Bank was ongoing.

“Malaysia has pursued, and will continue to pursue, action against international banks which we believe failed to carry out proper customer due diligence checks in relation to the movement of 1MDB funds by Low, his associates and/or proxies,” he said.

1MDB is currently in settlement talks with Deutsche Bank over the legal dispute.

Low has previously denied wrongdoing, and his current whereabouts are unknown. REUTERS

data.title: Court clears path for Frasersâ S$391.9 million Centrepoint en bloc deal
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The High Court on Thursday (Nov 19) has greenlit the collective sale of The Centrepoint rear block to Frasers Property for S$391.9 million, in granting a sale order for the property, The Business Times understands.

The ruling clears the way for Frasers to take full ownership of the rear block on completion, giving it scope to redevelop the Orchard Road site alongside neighbouring assets that it already owns.

The deal had hit a hitch in August, when the Strata Titles Board (STB) issued a stop order after two objections to the sale were not withdrawn during mediation. The collective sale committee then applied to the High Court for approval.

Both objections were withdrawn before Thursday’s hearing.

Wee Swee Teow LLP represented the owners in the collective sale, led by real estate partner Alan Tan, with the high court application led by partner Hui Choon Wai.

Frasers Property was awarded the tender for the rear block of The Centrepoint on Feb 27 for S$391.9 million, about 6.2 per cent below the guide price of S$418 million when the property was put on the market in January.

The Centrepoint comprises two components: a freehold front plot and a leasehold rear plot.

Frasers Property owns almost all – about 96 per cent – of The Centrepoint’s front block, which houses 151 retail units on a freehold plot.

Before the collective sale, the group also owned part of the rear block, which contains 66 apartments and 66 retail units on an L-shaped plot with around 52 years left on its 99-year lease. It reportedly held all the retail strata units and eight apartments, adding up to about 52 per cent of the strata area and about 85 per cent of the share value in the rear block.

The acquisition was a strategic move by Frasers Property to consolidate its ownership of the adjoining plots, paving the way for a larger redevelopment of prime Orchard Road site.

Frasers Property owns the neighbouring 51 Cuppage Road, a 10-storey office building connected to The Centrepoint by a link bridge. The group in August also acquired Cuppage Terrace next to The Centrepoint for S$175 million, citing plans to take a more coordinated approach to asset enhancement and long-term value creation.

The group could potentially amalgamate the sites to tap incentives under the Urban Redevelopment Authority’s Strategic Development Incentive Scheme, which encourages the redevelopment of ageing properties in key areas through more intensive land use.

The S$810 million collective sale of Thomson View condominium followed a similar path. The STB issued a stop order in March 2025 after mediation failed to resolve objections from six owners. The High Court approved the sale in July that year after all six withdrew their objections and the sale committee filed a further affidavit addressing the judge’s questions about whether the required mandate had been secured in time.

UOL, Singapore Land and CapitaLand Development subsequently launched Thomson Reserve, a 1,268-unit condominium project on the former Thomson View site, in October this year.

The development sold 1,143 units, or over 90 per cent of its total units, at an average price of S$2,900 per square foot over its launch weekend, making it the best-selling new private residential project in Singapore this year by the number of units sold at launch.
